cue.topic: Describe a festival or celebration in your country
bullets: what the festival is and when it takes place
what people do during the celebration
who you usually celebrate it with
and explain why it means so much to you

part2.model: I'd like to talk about Tet, the Lunar New Year festival, which is by far the biggest celebration in my country. It takes place in late January or February, depending on the lunar calendar, and it lasts about a week. Last year my friend Thao invited me to spend it with her family in a village near Hue, and it was the most memorable Tet I've ever had. The preparations began days earlier. We cleaned the house from top to bottom, hung branches of apricot blossom by the door, and spent an afternoon wrapping sticky rice cakes in banana leaves while her uncles argued cheerfully about the right way to fold them. On New Year's Eve the whole family sat down to a lavish meal, and at midnight we watched fireworks light up the sky. The next morning the children received lucky red envelopes, and everyone put on their best clothes to visit relatives and pay their respects at the family altar. Her little cousins ran around the courtyard in stiff new outfits, shrieking with excitement whenever someone handed them a sweet. What makes this festival special is that it brings generations together. People travel hundreds of kilometres to be home, and old arguments are forgotten. For me, it's a chance to wipe the slate clean and start the year with a positive outlook. Thao's grandmother even taught me a traditional recipe, which I still cook every year.

vocab.meaning: forget past problems and start again

questions.q: Why do some people feel it is important to preserve traditions?
questions.model: I think traditions act as an anchor in a rapidly changing world. They remind people where they come from and give communities a shared sense of belonging. For example, family rituals pass down values from one generation to the next. Without them, society could feel rather rootless. Personally, I believe we should keep the customs that bring people together and let go of those that have outlived their purpose, so that heritage stays alive rather than becoming a museum exhibit.

questions.q: Should governments fund the preservation of traditional festivals and heritage sites?
questions.model: Yes, up to a point. Heritage sites and festivals are part of the national story, and local communities rarely have the funds to maintain crumbling temples on their own. Public money can also create jobs for craftspeople and guides. Nevertheless, spending should be transparent, otherwise taxpayers may feel it is wasted. Personally, I'd back a partnership where the state covers essential repairs and private sponsors support events, so the burden is shared fairly.

questions.model: We would lose far more than just beautiful objects. Traditional crafts carry skills, stories and local knowledge that took centuries to develop, and once the last master dies, that expertise is almost impossible to rebuild. Communities might also lose a source of income and pride. To prevent this, schools could offer workshops, and consumers could be willing to pay a premium for handmade goods. It is really about valuing quality over speed.

On balance, I would say the threat is real but manageable if communities take pride in what makes them unique.

questions.q: Is it right for tourism to turn sacred ceremonies into commercial attractions?
questions.model: It's a delicate issue. On the one hand, tourism brings in vital revenue that helps communities maintain their customs. On the other hand, when sacred rituals are staged for crowds with cameras, they risk losing their authenticity and meaning. In my view, the key is respect. Visitors should follow local etiquette, and hosts should decide which ceremonies are open to outsiders. With clear boundaries, culture can be shared without being turned into a cheap spectacle.
